title: Is Russia's rival to Starlink failing? Here's what we know.
gist: Russia's Rassvet megaconstellation, run by Bureau 1440 as a domestic answer to Starlink, has launched 32 satellites across two 2026 launches but none has reached its designed 500-mile orbit, with at least three outright failures and several more stalled. Ukraine is striking the Soyuz factory and Plesetsk Cosmodrome to slow deployment, while the 12 satellites at 300 miles already give Russian forces up to 90-minute communication windows over Ukraine twice a day.

insights.claim: Two launches in March and July 2026 delivered 32 Rassvet satellites to low-Earth orbit, roughly 10 percent of the approximately 300 spacecraft Russia aims to have in orbit by the end of next year, against Bureau 1440's stated target of 924 satellites by 2035.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: The deployment rate implies the 300-satellite goal requires roughly 16 more launches in about a year — a cadence Russia's launch and manufacturing base has never demonstrated.
insights.locator: The Rassvet program, often billed as Russia’s answer to Starlink

insights.claim: None of the 32 Rassvet satellites launched so far has reached the 500-mile (800-kilometer) orbit they were designed to operate in; the highest altitude achieved is a little more than 300 miles, with 12 of the first 16 settled there.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
entities: Institute for the Study of War
insights.so_what: Zero satellites at design altitude after two launches is a hard, independently observable metric for tracking whether Russia's Starlink substitute is viable.
insights.locator: But none of the 32 satellites launched so far

insights.claim: At least three of the first 32 Rassvet satellites likely suffered outright failures: one from the March batch never maneuvered significantly and reentered in June, and two from the July batch never maneuvered and appear headed for reentry.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: A roughly 10 percent hard-failure rate on the first cohort is in line with early Starlink, but Russia lacks the launch cadence to iterate out of it quickly.

insights.claim: SpaceX's first 60 Starlink prototypes suffered about a 13 percent failure rate over time with roughly 5 percent failing almost immediately, the next 420 satellites dropped to about 3 percent, and the current Starlink Version 2 generation runs about 0.01 percent according to Jonathan McDowell's tabulations.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: The Starlink learning curve is the correct benchmark for judging any new megaconstellation: expect double-digit early failures and judge the operator on how fast the rate falls.

insights.claim: The US Space Development Agency's own first 42 operational data relay satellites for missile targeting and command and control hit thermal and propulsion problems after launching last year and have taken longer than anticipated to raise their orbits.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Orbit-raising trouble is not uniquely Russian — a caution against over-reading Rassvet's stumbles as evidence of terminal decline.
insights.locator: The US military’s Space Development Agency

insights.claim: The author flags an alternative benign explanation: Russia may have deliberately abandoned the 500-mile plan or be parking satellites low to let orbital planes drift into final alignment, noting Starlink itself flies closer to 300 miles with performance benefits but requiring more satellites for global coverage.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Don't treat altitude shortfall alone as proof of failure; the diagnostic signal is whether satellites stop maneuvering entirely.
insights.locator: However, there’s a lot we don’t know.

insights.claim: Russia's entire satellite manufacturing sector has produced at best just a few dozen spacecraft per year since the fall of the Soviet Union, a structural ceiling far below megaconstellation requirements.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Manufacturing throughput, not launch or capital, is the binding constraint on Russia's constellation ambitions — the metric to watch is annual satellite production, not launch announcements.
insights.quote: It turned out we weren’t ready for this
insights.locator: What we do know is that putting a megaconstellation into orbit is hard

insights.claim: Russia's satellite industry has long suffered chronic underfunding, corruption, production bottlenecks and reliability problems, now compounded by Ukrainian cyber, drone and missile attacks on space infrastructure and by personnel and funding redirected from the space program to the war effort.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: The constraints are cumulative and structural, arguing that Rassvet slips well past its stated timelines regardless of the current orbit-raising questions.
insights.locator: It’s not all that surprising that those hopes failed

insights.claim: SpaceX cut off access in February to the Starlink network by unregistered user terminals in Ukraine to block Russia's illicit use of satellite communications, and the first Rassvet launch came the following month, offering Russian commanders hope of a domestic replacement.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: A commercial operator's terminal-level enforcement action created direct military demand for a sovereign constellation — a precedent for how connectivity dependence gets weaponized.
insights.locator: Russian forces are clamoring for Rassvet

insights.claim: The 12 Rassvet satellites currently at 300 miles are arranged in a formation that brings them over Ukraine twice per day for communication windows of up to 90 minutes, which the Institute for the Study of War says still enables more precise strikes with remotely controlled unmanned systems.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
entities: Institute for the Study of War
insights.so_what: Even a broken constellation delivers usable intermittent military capability — partial deployment is not zero capability.
insights.quote: The existing Rassvet satellite constellation still presents a threat to Ukraine as it may allow Russian forces to conduct more precise strikes against Ukraine using remotely controlled unmanned systems
insights.locator: The 12 Rassvet satellites currently flying at 300 miles

insights.claim: It will take 16 more launches to bring Rassvet's coverage over Ukraine anywhere close to continuous, and Ukraine has struck the factory that builds the Soyuz rockets needed for those launches while dispatching drones against the Plesetsk Cosmodrome launch pad.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Space-industrial infrastructure has become a legitimate deep-strike target class; expect counter-space to migrate further toward attacking factories and pads rather than satellites.

insights.claim: Soyuz rockets are the workhorse for Russia's entire space program — launching navigation satellites, spy spacecraft and crew missions to the International Space Station — so strikes on their production facility carry consequences well beyond Rassvet.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: A single production chokepoint links Russian civil, military and crewed spaceflight; degrade it and all three slip together.
insights.locator: Earlier this month, Ukraine struck the factory
